title: Build one million new homes
detail: Release public and private land together with regions and town halls. A new land law (*Ley del Suelo*) would speed up planning, social housing could go on land reserved for public facilities (*suelo dotacional*), offices could become affordable homes, and building permits would be due within 3 months under "positive silence" (*silencio positivo*, no answer means yes). The programme gives no deadline for the million.
c: Spain currently finishes around 100,000 homes a year; a million in four years would mean 2.5 times that, with shortages of workers and land. The programme sets no deadline. Land and permits belong to regions and town halls, so central government can only speed things up in part.

s.t: Housing Ministry: Observatorio de Vivienda y Suelo, annual bulletin 2024 (La Moncloa)

title: Repeal the 2023 Housing Law (*Ley de Vivienda*)
detail: Scrap the law, including its "stressed market areas" (*zonas tensionadas*) and rent price index, which the programme says brought more intervention, uncertainty and fewer homes to rent. It does not say what would replace the law.
c: Repeal needs an ordinary law, and PP plus Vox would have the votes. But PP-run regions never declared stressed areas, so the market effect would be smaller than promised. The replacement is not described.
pos: Landlords get predictable rules, and some homes may move back from seasonal and tourist lets to long-term rental.
neg: In Catalonia, where caps apply, tenants lose protection against steep rises at renewal. More supply is not guaranteed: building is held back by land and permits, not by this law.

title: 4% VAT on a first home for under-40s
detail: Cut VAT (*IVA*) on a first new home from 10% to 4% for buyers under 40, payable in instalments along with the mortgage. Agree with regions a lower transfer tax (*ITP*) on resale first homes for young buyers, and extend to 4 years the window to reinvest the proceeds of selling a main home (*vivienda habitual*) tax-free.
c: An age-based 4% rate has to fit the EU VAT directive. Paying VAT in mortgage instalments is non-standard; the tax agency has no such tool. With supply short, a demand subsidy mostly lifts prices.
pos: A new home gets about 6% cheaper (VAT 10% to 4%), making it easier for young people to stop renting.
neg: With supply short, part of the relief passes into the seller's price. The Treasury loses revenue, and the help goes to people who can already buy rather than the poorest.

s.t: Directive (EU) 2022/542 on VAT rates (BOE copy of the OJEU)
Ley 37/1992 on VAT (BOE)

title: State guarantee for the deposit
detail: Extend a public guarantee (*aval público*) covering up to 20% of the price to buyers under 40 (possibly up to 50), so the mortgage can also cover the deposit.
c: A similar ICO guarantee for young buyers has run since 2023, so this is an extension. Easy to do; part of the help will be absorbed by higher prices.
pos: Removes the main barrier for young buyers, saving up a 20% deposit. A similar ICO guarantee has already worked since 2023.
neg: More demand without new supply pushes prices up. The state takes on credit risk: in a downturn the Treasury pays out on guarantees.

s.t: Council of Ministers, 9 May 2023: ICO guarantee line for first homes (La Moncloa)

title: Squatters out within 48 hours
detail: A new law so owners get a home back within 48 hours of a court order, and owners' associations can go to court themselves (reform of the *Ley de Propiedad Horizontal*). While a home is occupied, the owner would not pay utilities or taxes, and the squatter's town-hall registration (*empadronamiento*) would be void.
c: LO 1/2025 already sped up squatting cases. Entering a home requires a court decision (art. 18.2 of the Constitution), and 48 hours depends on court workload, not on the wording of a law. Realistic only with more judges.
pos: Owners and neighbours are protected from unlawful occupation, which builds confidence in letting homes.
neg: Risk of wrongful evictions of vulnerable families without a check of their social situation. Courts are already overloaded, so 48 hours is hard to guarantee. In our estimate, the effect on the housing market would be minimal.

s.t: Ley Orgánica 1/2025 on the efficiency of the justice system (BOE)
Spanish Constitution, art. 18 (BOE)

title: Index income tax bands to inflation
detail: Index the income tax (*IRPF*) scale to inflation (*deflactar la tarifa*) and update its main allowances, so that price rises (almost 30% in recent years, the programme says) stop acting as a hidden tax increase.
c: Economically sound and technically simple. But it costs several billion euros a year, and EU fiscal rules limit room for manoeuvre. More likely in stages.
pos: Removes the hidden tax rise caused by inflation ("bracket creep"), making the tax fairer.
neg: Higher earners gain more in absolute terms. The Treasury loses several billion euros a year with no stated offset.

title: Income tax discount for 18–35s: 100/75/50/25%
detail: Employees and self-employed people aged 18–35 get a discount on their first four years of income tax: 100% in year one, then 75%, 50% and 25%. It would apply from the first tax return after the law passes.
c: Easy to introduce by law. An age-based discount could be challenged as unequal treatment (arts. 14 and 31 of the Constitution), and it creates an incentive to book income in young people's names. No cost estimate is given.
pos: A strong incentive for young people to work in Spain rather than leave; it may draw emigrants back.
neg: Costly and unequal: two identical workers pay different tax only because of age. Open to abuse through self-employment. The effect on emigration is unproven.

s.t: Spanish Constitution, art. 14 (BOE)
Spanish Constitution, art. 31 (BOE)

title: 0% VAT on basic food
detail: For as long as the inflation crisis lasts, 0% VAT on basic food, including meat, fish and tinned food. The programme gives no full list.
c: Spain already applied 0% on basic food in 2023–24, and EU law allows it. Banco de España and the CNMC found the 2023 cut was passed on to prices almost in full; the Fedea think tank estimated that half the savings went to the best-off 40% of households.
pos: Cheaper food, especially for poorer households, where food is a large share of spending.
neg: Half the savings went to the best-off 40% of households in 2023, according to Fedea. The measure is costly, and a temporary tax break is politically hard to end later.

s.t: Banco de España, Working Paper 2417 (2024): VAT cut pass-through to prices
CNMC, 10 Aug 2023: study of the VAT cut pass-through to food prices
Fedea (think tank), López Laborda et al., Apuntes 2023/02: who gained from the VAT cut

title: No social security fees for new *autónomos* in year one
detail: New self-employed workers (*autónomos*) pay no social security contribution (*cuota*) in their first year, and none in the second year if their income is below the minimum wage (*SMI*). Their main home would be protected from creditors by default.
c: A flat rate (*tarifa plana*) of €80 a month already exists. A full zero costs more and encourages employers to move staff into bogus self-employment. Doable by ordinary law.
pos: A lower barrier to going self-employed: more start-ups and more work done legally.
neg: Fewer contributions mean a smaller future pension for the self-employed person. Firms may push employees into "false self-employment".

s.t: Real Decreto-ley 13/2022: self-employed contributions and flat rate (BOE)

title: Identify irregular arrivals within 7 days, then fast returns
detail: People who cross the border irregularly would be identified and security-checked within a week at most, then quickly processed for asylum or returned, with shorter deadlines in emergencies under the new EU mechanism.
c: The EU Pact on Migration and Asylum (applying from June 2026) itself introduces screening of up to 7 days, so this point partly just implements it. Fast returns depend on countries of origin agreeing to take their nationals back.
pos: Faster procedures and fewer people left in legal limbo.
neg: Seven days is short for a proper check: risk of expelling people entitled to asylum, and of European Court of Human Rights rulings against Spain. Returns depend on countries of origin.

s.t: Regulation (EU) 2024/1356 on border screening (BOE copy of the OJEU)

title: Ban mass regularisations; *arraigo* only as an exception
detail: The Immigration Law (*Ley de Extranjería*) would forbid mass, blanket regularisations; *arraigo* (residence based on settled ties to Spain) would become an exceptional, case-by-case route. Town-hall registration (*empadronamiento*) alone would not give a right to non-emergency cash benefits.
c: The Immigration Law is an organic law: 176 votes, realistic with Vox. Permits already granted cannot be withdrawn. Narrowing *arraigo* would leave hundreds of thousands without status, but with no real way to remove them either.
pos: Sends the signal that irregular entry does not lead to legal status, which weakens smuggling networks.
neg: Hundreds of thousands of people stay undocumented and in the shadow economy: less tax and fewer contributions, more exploitation.

s.t: Ley Orgánica 4/2000 on foreigners' rights (BOE)
Spanish Constitution, art. 81 (BOE)

title: 4,500 more GPs and better conditions for doctors
detail: At least 4,500 extra doctors in primary care (*Atención Primaria*), more specialist training places (*MIR*), better pay and working conditions, and a separate negotiating table for doctors. Shorter on-call shifts (*guardias*) would come through workforce planning with the regions; no date or size is given.
c: The 4,500 doctors are not on the market: training a family doctor (degree plus MIR) takes years. More MIR places pay off after 2030, and regions do the hiring.
pos: Shorter waits in primary care, and better conditions mean fewer doctors leaving for abroad.
neg: Costly, and health care is run by the regions: the state pays but does not manage. Training doctors takes years.

title: Repeal the Amnesty Law and limit pardons
detail: Repeal the Amnesty Law (*Ley de Amnistía*), ban pardons (*indultos*) as payment for supporting a government, and pass a new Pardons Law with objective criteria, excluding corruption, terrorism and crimes against the constitutional order.
c: The law can be repealed (176 votes), but an amnesty already applied cannot be undone: the Constitution bars unfavourable retroactive laws (art. 9.3). In 2025 the Constitutional Court found the law largely constitutional. A new Pardons Law is realistic.

s.t: Ley Orgánica 1/2024 on amnesty (BOE)
Spanish Constitution, art. 9 (BOE)
Constitutional Court ruling 137/2025 on the amnesty (BOE)

title: Drop the nuclear phase-out timetable
detail: Within 100 days, start extending the lives of the Almaraz, Ascó, Vandellós, Cofrentes and Trillo plants (with approval from the nuclear safety council, *Consejo de Seguridad Nuclear*), rewrite the national energy and climate plan (*PNIEC*) "with realism", and back a nuclear strategy including small modular reactors.
c: An extension needs the owners to apply and a CSN report. At its owners' request Almaraz has already been extended to June 2030 (Orden TED/864/2026); the other plants need new applications, and the companies want lower taxes.
pos: Keeps about a fifth of electricity output (about 19% in 2025, according to REE) emission-free, with stable capacity for the grid.
neg: Needs investment by the owners and CSN approval; nuclear waste storage remains unsolved. In hours of surplus power, more solar and wind gets curtailed, and the incentive to build storage weakens.

s.t: Orden TED/864/2026: Almaraz extended to 8 June 2030 (BOE)
REE: 2025 year-end data, generation mix
